paragraphs.title: The Weight of Suffering and the Wish for Death

answers: Heavier than the sand of the sea
easy.explanation: Job says his calamity would be heavier than the sand of the sea.
easy.q: How does Job describe the weight of his grief and calamity?

easy.explanation: Job says the arrows of the Almighty are within him.
easy.q: What does Job say is within him?

answers: Destroy him and cut him off
easy.explanation: Job wishes that God would destroy him and cut him off.
easy.q: What does Job ask God to do?

answers: Because his suffering is extremely heavy
medium.explanation: His words are overwhelmed by the weight of his grief and calamity.
medium.q: Why does Job say that his words are swallowed up?

answers: Setting themselves in array against him
medium.explanation: Job says that the terrors of God are arranged against him.
medium.q: What are the “terrors of God” doing against Job?

answers: He compares himself to a king
He compares himself to a stream
He asks whether a wild ass brays when it has grass or an ox lows over its fodder
medium.explanation: Job argues that animals do not cry out without a reason, and neither does he.
medium.q: Which comparison shows that Job’s cry has a real cause?

answers: They suggest that his suffering has a genuine cause
They describe his work with cattle
They praise the strength of animals
challenge.explanation: Like animals that cry out when they lack food, Job is crying out because of real suffering.
challenge.q: How do the wild ass and ox questions support Job’s complaint?

answers: To show that his situation offers no pleasantness or comfort
To explain why he is hungry
challenge.explanation: The food images express his disgust and lack of comfort.
challenge.q: Why does Job mention unsavoury food and the white of an egg?

answers: As a possible hope and consolation
challenge.explanation: Job longs for God to end his life and says that this would bring him comfort.
challenge.q: How is death presented in verses 8–10?

paragraphs.title: Human Frailty in the Face of Suffering

answers: What strength he has to hope
What strength he has to build a house
What strength he has to win a war
easy.explanation: Job asks what his strength is that he should continue to hope.
easy.q: What does Job ask about his strength?

easy.explanation: Job asks whether his strength is the strength of stones or whether his flesh is brass.
easy.q: What materials does Job say he is not made of?

easy.explanation: Job asks whether wisdom has been driven quite from him.
easy.q: What does Job say has been driven from him?

answers: To show that he is wealthy
To emphasize human weakness and limited endurance
medium.explanation: He is not made of unbreakable stone or metal, but is a frail human being.
medium.q: Why does Job mention stones and brass?

medium.explanation: Job asks whether he still has help or strength within himself.
medium.q: In this passage, what does “help” most closely mean?

answers: He says they brought him food
He moves from his weakness to the absence of help
He announces that he needs no one
medium.explanation: After describing his weakness, Job asks why help and wisdom have failed him.
medium.q: How do Job’s questions lead to his complaint about others?

answers: He struggles both to keep hoping and to endure suffering
He is certain he will recover immediately
He wants to defeat his friends
challenge.explanation: Job doubts both his ability to continue hoping and his ability to continue suffering.
challenge.q: What is implied by Job’s mention of both hope and strength?

answers: Job first describes the loss of help and then the failure of pity
Job returns to speaking about animals
Job describes his wealth and then his home
challenge.explanation: The lack of help leads to his complaint that pity is not shown to the afflicted.
challenge.q: What is the connection between verses 13 and 14?

answers: The afflicted are denied pity and the fear of the Almighty is forsaken
challenge.explanation: Job says that pity should be shown to the afflicted, but that the fear of the Almighty has been abandoned.
challenge.q: What is Job’s main criticism in verse 14?

easy.explanation: Job says that his brethren have dealt deceitfully as a brook.
easy.q: What does Job compare his brethren to?

answers: They freeze, vanish, and dry up
easy.explanation: The streams are blackened by ice, vanish when warm, and are consumed by heat.
easy.q: What happens to the streams described by Job?

answers: The troops of Tema and the companies of Sheba
easy.explanation: Job says that the troops of Tema looked and the companies of Sheba waited for them.

answers: Because they cannot be relied upon when needed
medium.explanation: The streams appear promising but disappear when travelers need water, like Job’s friends’ support.
medium.q: Why are failing streams a fitting picture of Job’s friends?

medium.explanation: The streams disappear when the weather becomes warm.
medium.q: What does “vanish” mean in the description of the streams?

answers: Both look for water or comfort and meet disappointment
medium.explanation: The travelers hoped for water, while Job hoped for comfort, but both were disappointed.
medium.q: What is similar about the caravans and Job?

answers: The unreliability of the friends’ help
challenge.explanation: The streams look useful but fail to provide water when it is needed.
challenge.q: What does the image of streams freezing and drying up emphasize?

answers: They trusted streams that supplied no water
challenge.explanation: They hoped for water but came to a place where the streams had failed.
challenge.q: Why were the companies of Tema and Sheba ashamed?

answers: Job begins with the stream comparison and ends by saying his friends have become a disappointment
Job returns to describing his sickness
challenge.explanation: The passage begins by comparing his friends to unreliable streams and ends by saying they are useless to him.
challenge.q: What is the connection between verses 15 and 21?

paragraphs.title: What Job Never Asked of His Friends

easy.explanation: Job asks whether he ever said, “Bring unto me” or “Give a reward for me.”
easy.q: Did Job ask his friends to bring him a gift or money?

answers: Deliver him from the enemy and redeem him from the mighty
Heal the diseases of the field
easy.explanation: Job says he did not ask them to deliver or redeem him.
easy.q: What did Job not ask them to do?

answers: Why his friends withdrew from him
easy.explanation: He cannot understand why they have abandoned him when he asked them for nothing.
easy.q: What is Job trying to understand through these questions?

medium.explanation: Job denies asking for a gift, a reward, rescue from the enemy, or redemption from the mighty.
medium.q: Which series of requests does Job deny making?

medium.explanation: Job asks whether he requested a reward from their substance, meaning payment or material help.
medium.q: What does “reward” refer to in this context?

answers: It shows that he did not demand special material help from them
It proves that he is not suffering
It shows that he is angry with everyone
medium.explanation: Job argues that his friends abandoned him even though he made no costly request.
medium.q: Why is it important to Job that he asked for nothing?

answers: He wants comfort, but his friends act as if he demanded costly rescue
He wants wealth, but they bring water
He wants silence, but they refuse to speak
challenge.explanation: Job explains that he never required money or military rescue, so their withdrawal makes no sense.
challenge.q: What is the main contrast in Job’s words?

answers: They show that his friends’ withdrawal is not justified by any request he made
They show that he has rejected all friendship
They prove that his friends rescued him
challenge.explanation: By listing what he did not ask for, Job emphasizes that their abandonment is unjustified.
challenge.q: How do the questions in verses 22–23 strengthen Job’s complaint?

answers: They failed to give him the help he demanded
They withdrew even though he did not ask them to pay, redeem, or fight for him
challenge.explanation: Job stresses that he never asked them for material or military sacrifice.
challenge.q: What is Job’s main criticism of his friends here?

easy.explanation: Job says, “Teach me,” and asks them to show him wherein he has erred.
easy.q: What does Job ask his friends to show him?

easy.explanation: Job asks, “How forcible are right words!”
easy.q: What kind of words does Job value?

answers: Overwhelming the fatherless and digging a pit for a friend
easy.explanation: Job says that they overwhelm the fatherless and dig a pit for their friend.
easy.q: What are Job’s friends accused of doing?

answers: He is willing to listen if they show him his error
He immediately tells them to be silent
medium.explanation: Job says, “Teach me, and I will hold my tongue,” if they explain his error.
medium.q: How does Job respond to possible correction from his friends?

medium.explanation: Job says such speeches are “as wind.”
medium.q: What are “the speeches of one that is desperate” compared to?

answers: Genuine correction explains the error, while empty reproof merely harms without helping
Empty reproof is spoken only at night
medium.explanation: Job welcomes clear instruction but rejects arguments that are empty and useless.
medium.q: What is the difference between genuine correction and empty reproof?

answers: The fatherless represent the weak and vulnerable
The fatherless are the friends’ enemies
The fatherless are richer than the friends
challenge.explanation: Harming the fatherless portrays the friends as attacking someone vulnerable instead of helping.
challenge.q: Why does mentioning the fatherless make Job’s accusation more serious?

answers: They are spoken to a broken person without providing real help
They are written upon the wind
challenge.explanation: Job describes their words as insubstantial and useless to someone in distress.
challenge.q: What is implied by describing desperate words as “wind”?

answers: He rejects every kind of criticism
He accepts accurate correction but rejects empty and hurtful accusations
challenge.explanation: Job asks his friends to identify his error but objects to unsupported, harmful words.
challenge.q: What attitude toward criticism does Job show in verses 24–27?

paragraphs.title: An Invitation to Examine His Integrity

easy.explanation: Job tells them to be content and look upon him.
easy.q: What does Job ask his friends to do?

easy.explanation: Job says it should be evident to them if he lies.
easy.q: What does Job ask them to examine?

easy.explanation: Job asks whether there is iniquity in his tongue.
easy.q: What does Job say about his tongue?

answers: So they can examine his claims personally
So they can fight his enemies
So they can bring him gifts
medium.explanation: He wants them to face him and judge whether he is lying.
medium.q: Why does Job ask his friends to look directly at him?

medium.explanation: Iniquity means moral wrongdoing or injustice.
medium.q: What does “iniquity” mean in this passage?

answers: Job asks them to reconsider their judgment and says that his speech is not unjust
Job returns to speaking about streams
medium.explanation: He urges them to return to a fair judgment and asks whether his tongue contains iniquity.
medium.q: What is the connection between verses 29 and 30?

answers: He believes his words can be tested and found free of wrong
He does not know what he has said
challenge.explanation: Job openly invites examination because he is confident that his speech is honest.
challenge.q: What does Job’s invitation to examine him reveal about his confidence?

answers: Job asks them to reconsider their unjust treatment and examine his case again
Job asks them to go home silently
Job asks them to repeat their words
challenge.explanation: Job calls on his friends to turn back from their unjust judgment and reassess him.
challenge.q: What does “Return, I pray you” mean in the argument?

answers: By expressing confidence that his mouth speaks honestly about his calamity
challenge.explanation: Job insists that his tongue is not unjust and that he can discern the perverse or wrong thing.
challenge.q: How does Job’s speech end in this passage?
